On Godbersen’s Conjecture

S. Artstein-Avidan    K. Einhorn    D.Y. Florentin    Y. Ostrover
Abstract

We provide a natural generalization of a geometric conjecture of Fáry and Rédei regarding the volume of the convex hull of K⊂ℝnK\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, and its negative image −K-K. We show that it implies Godbersen’s conjecture regarding the mixed volumes of the convex bodies KK and −K-K. We then use the same type of reasoning to produce the currently best known upper bound for the mixed volumes V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])V(K[j],-K[n-j]), which is not far from Godbersen’s conjectured bound. To this end we prove a certain functional inequality generalizing Colesanti’s difference function inequality.

1 Introduction and results

In this note we consider convex bodies K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, that is, compact convex sets with non-empty interior. The well known Rogers–Shephard bound for the volume of the so called “difference body”, K−K={x−y|x,y∈K}K-K=\{x-y\,|\,x,y\in K\}, states that

Vol⁡(K−K)≤(2​nn)​Vol​(K).{\rm Vol}(K-K)\leq\binom{2n}{n}{\rm Vol}(K). (1)

This inequality was proved by Rogers and Shephard in [11], where it was also shown that equality is attained only for simplices. By a simplex we mean the convex hull of n+1n+1 affinely independent points in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Chakerian simplified their argument in [2], and in [12] they gave another variant of the proof, which we address in the appendix of this text.

A conjectured strengthening of the difference body inequality was suggested in 1938 by Godbersen [8] (and independently by Makai Jr. [9]).

Conjecture 1.1.

For any convex body K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and any 1≤j≤n−11\leq j\leq n-1,

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])≤(nj)​Vol​(K),V(K[j],-K[n-j])\leq\binom{n}{j}{\rm Vol}(K), (2)

with equality attained only for simplices.

Here V⁡(K1,…,Kn)V(K_{1},\ldots,K_{n}) denotes the mixed volume of the nn convex bodies K1,…,KnK_{1},\ldots,K_{n}, and V⁡(K⁡[j],T⁡[n−j])V(K[j],T[n-j]) denotes the mixed volume of jj copies of the convex body KK and n−jn-j copies of the convex body TT. We recall that for convex bodies K1,…,Km⊂ℝnK_{1},\ldots,K_{m}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, and non-negative real numbers λ1,…,λm\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{m}, a classical result of Minkowski states that the volume of ∑λi​Ki\sum\lambda_{i}K_{i} is a homogeneous polynomial of degree nn in λi\lambda_{i},

Vol(∑i=1mλiKi)=∑i1,…,in=1mλi1⋯λinV(Ki1,…,Kin),{\rm Vol}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}K_{i}\right)=\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{n}=1}^{m}\lambda_{i_{1}}\cdots\lambda_{i_{n}}V(K_{i_{1}},\dots,K_{i_{n}}), (3)

and the coefficient V⁡(Ki1,…,Kin)V(K_{i_{1}},\dots,K_{i_{n}}), which depends solely on Ki1,…,KinK_{i_{1}},\ldots,K_{i_{n}}, is called the mixed volume of Ki1,…,KinK_{i_{1}},\ldots,K_{i_{n}}. The mixed volume is a non-negative, translation invariant function, monotone with respect to set inclusion, invariant under permutations of its arguments, and positively homogeneous in each argument. Moreover, one has V⁡(K⁡[n])=Vol⁡(K)V(K[n])={\rm Vol}(K). For further information on mixed volumes and their properties, see Section §5.1 of [14].

The cases j=1j=1 and j=n−1j=n-1 of Conjecture 1.1 follow from the fact that −K⊂n​K-K\subset nK for bodies with center of mass at the origin (see [1], page 57). The same argument gives the bound

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])≤nmin⁡{j,n−j}​Vol​(K),V(K[j],-K[n-j])\leq n^{\min\{j,n-j\}}{\rm Vol}(K),

for 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n. The only other cases for which Conjecture 1.1 is verified, are simplices (which are the equality case) and bodies of constant width, as shown in [8]. Godbersen’s conjecture is indeed a strengthening of the difference body inequality (1) since, if Conjecture 1.1 holds true, one may write

Vol⁡(K−K)=∑j=0n(nj)​V​(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])≤∑j=0n(nj)2​Vol​(K)=(2​nn)​Vol​(K).{\rm Vol}(K-K)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}V(K[j],-K[n-j])\leq\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}^{2}{\rm Vol}(K)=\binom{2n}{n}{\rm Vol}(K).

In 1950, Fáry and Rédei [6] conjectured that for all convex bodies KK of fixed volume, one has

minx∈K⁡Vol⁡((K−x)∨(x−K))≤minx∈S⁡Vol⁡((S−x)∨(x−S)),\min_{x\in K}{\rm Vol}((K-x)\vee(x-K))\leq\min_{x\in S}{\rm Vol}((S-x)\vee(x-S)), (4)

where SS is a simplex with Vol⁡(S)=Vol⁡(K){\rm Vol}(S)={\rm Vol}(K). Here, A∨BA\vee B denotes the convex hull of the sets AA and BB. Moreover, they showed that the right-hand side of (4) is precisely (n[n/2])​Vol​(S)\binom{n}{[n/2]}{\rm Vol}(S). We conjecture the following generalization of (4).

Conjecture 1.2.

For any convex body K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], there exists x∈Kx\in K such that

Vol⁡((1−λ)​(K−x)∨λ⁡(x−K))≤Vol⁡((1−λ)​S∨−λ​S),{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)(K-x)\vee\lambda(x-K))\leq{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)S\vee-\lambda S), (5)

where SS is a centered simplex, and Vol⁡(S)=Vol⁡(K){\rm Vol}(S)={\rm Vol}(K).

Note that the case λ=1/2\lambda=1/2 implies the above mentioned conjecture by Fáry and Rédei (since for the simplex, the convex hull of minimal volume is attained when it is centered, see [4]). The numerical value of the right-hand side of (5)(\ref{GFR-Conj}) can be computed explicitly (see Section 2), so that Conjecture 1.2 would give a numerical upper bound for the quantity on the left-hand side of (5)(\ref{GFR-Conj}). Moreover, we remark that in dimension n=2n=2, Conjecture 1.2 holds true (see Section 4 for a discussion of the planar case).

Our first result in this paper states that Conjecture 1.2 implies Godbersen’s conjecture.

Theorem 1.3.

Conjecture 1.2 implies Conjecture 1.1.

Our second result is, to the best of our knowledge, the smallest upper bound for V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])V(K[j],-K[n-j]) currently known for 2<j<n−22<j<n-2.

Theorem 1.4.

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body, and 1≤j≤n−11\leq j\leq n-1. Then

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])≤nnjj​(n−j)n−j​Vol​(K)≃(nj)​2​π​j⁡(n−j)n​Vol​(K).V(K[j],-K[n-j])\leq\frac{n^{n}}{j^{j}(n-j)^{n-j}}{\rm Vol}(K)\simeq\binom{n}{j}\sqrt{2\pi\,\frac{j(n-j)}{n}}{\rm Vol}(K).

The proof requires some preparation. Rogers and Shephard showed in [12] that if 0∈K0\in K, then

Vol⁡(K∨−K)≤2n​Vol​(K),{\rm Vol}(K\vee-K)\leq 2^{n}{\rm Vol}(K), (6)

and that the bound is attained only when KK is a simplex with 00 as a vertex. Another proof for this bound was given by Colesanti in [3] (see Section 3 below). Colesanti’s proof is based on a functional analogue of the difference body, which he calls the “difference function”. Using monotonicity of mixed volumes, (6)(\ref{RS-ineq-conv-hull}) implies that for every 1≤j≤n−11\leq j\leq n-1,

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])≤Vol⁡(K∨−K)≤2n​Vol​(K).V(K[j],-K[n-j])\leq{\rm Vol}(K\vee-K)\leq 2^{n}{\rm Vol}(K).

Our next result generalizes inequality (6)(\ref{RS-ineq-conv-hull}).

Theorem 1.5.

For any convex body K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} containing the origin and every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]

Vol⁡((1−λ)​K∨−λ​K)≤Vol⁡(K).{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K)\leq{\rm Vol}(K). (7)

Theorem 1.4 is an immediate corollary of Theorem 1.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.4:

Let 1≤j≤n−11\leq j\leq n-1, and set λ=(n−j)/n\lambda=(n-j)/n. Assume without loss of generality that 0∈K0\in K. Since (1−λ)​K(1-\lambda)K and −λ​K-\lambda K are contained in (1−λ)​K∨−λ​K(1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K, the monotonicity and homogeneity properties of the mixed volume imply:

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])\displaystyle V(K[j],-K[n-j]) =\displaystyle= 1(1−λ)j​λn−j​V​((1−λ)​K​[j],−λ​K​[n−j])\displaystyle\frac{1}{(1-\lambda)^{j}\lambda^{n-j}}V((1-\lambda)K[j],-\lambda K[n-j])
≤\displaystyle\leq 1(1−λ)j​λn−j​Vol​((1−λ)​K∨−λ​K)≤1(1−λ)j​λn−j​Vol​(K),\displaystyle\frac{1}{(1-\lambda)^{j}\lambda^{n-j}}{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K)\leq\frac{1}{(1-\lambda)^{j}\lambda^{n-j}}{\rm Vol}(K),

where the last inequality follows from Theorem 1.5. Plugging in our choice of λ\lambda yields precisely the desired bound of the theorem. ∎

Theorem 1.5 follows as a special case (where K=(1−λ)​K′K=(1-\lambda)K^{\prime}, L=λ​K′L=\lambda K^{\prime}, and θ=λ\theta=\lambda) from the following theorem, which is a variation of a result by Rogers and Shephard [12].

Theorem 1.6.

Let K,L⊆ℝnK,L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be two convex bodies such that 0∈K∩L0\in K\cap L. For every θ∈[0,1],\theta\in[0,1],

Vol⁡(L∨−K)​Vol​(θ​K∩(1−θ)​L)≤Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L).{\rm Vol}(L\vee-K)\,{\rm Vol}(\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L)\leq{\rm Vol}(K){\rm Vol}(L).

We will prove in the appendix that equality in Theorem 1.6 holds if and only if KK and LL are simplices with a common vertex at the origin and such that (1−θ)​L=θ​K(1-\theta)L=\theta K. Likewise, in Theorem 1.5, equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex with a vertex at the origin.

We offer two different proofs of Theorem 1.6. The first follows from a functional inequality which we turn now to describe. A second proof, which closely follows Rogers and Shephard’s original argument from [12] and is more geometric in nature, is presented in the appendix of this paper for completeness. We start with the notion of a “λ\lambda-difference function”.

Definition 1.7.

Let λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), and f,g:ℝn→ℝ+f,g\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{+}. The λ\lambda-difference function Δλf,g:ℝn→ℝ+\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{+} associated with ff and gg is defined by

Δλf,g​(z)=sup(1−λ)​x+λ​y=zf1−λ​(x1−λ)​gλ​(−yλ).\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}(z)=\sup_{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y=z}f^{1-\lambda}\left(\tfrac{x}{1-\lambda}\right)g^{\lambda}\left({\tfrac{-y}{\lambda}}\right).
Theorem 1.8.

Let f,g:ℝn→ℝ+f,g:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{+} be log-concave functions, and λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1). Then

∫ℝnΔλf,g​∫ℝnfλ​g1−λ≤∫ℝnf​∫ℝng.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f^{\lambda}g^{1-\lambda}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g. (8)

The proof of Theorem 1.8 is similar to Colesanti’s proof of Theorem 1.1 in [3]. An immediate corollary of Theorem 1.8 is the following result. Let K∘K^{\circ} stand for the polar body of KK (see definition below).

Theorem 1.9.

Let K,L⊂ℝnK,L\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} be convex bodies. Then

Vol⁡(K∨−L)​Vol​((K∘+L∘)∘)≤Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L).{\rm Vol}(K\vee-L)\,{\rm Vol}((K^{\circ}+L^{\circ})^{\circ})\leq{\rm Vol}(K)\,{\rm Vol}(L).

Note that Theorem 1.9 it strictly stronger than Theorem 1.6. Indeed, one can readily check that for every θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1], one has θ​K∩(1−θ)​L⊆(K∘+L∘)∘\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L\subseteq(K^{\circ}+L^{\circ})^{\circ}.

Notations: A convex body with center of mass at the origin is said to be centered. Given a convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, we denote by hK:ℝn→ℝh_{K}\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} its support function, that is, the 1-homogeneous convex function given by hK​(u)=sup{⟨x,u⟩|x∈K}h_{K}(u)=\sup\{\langle x,u\rangle\ |\ x\in K\}. The polar body of KK is defined as K∘={y∈ℝn|⟨x,y⟩≤1,∀x∈K}K^{\circ}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;|\;\langle x,y\rangle\leq 1,\forall x\in K\}, and is also a convex body. The convex indicator function 𝟙K∞\mathds{1}_{K}^{\infty} of KK is defined to be zero for x∈Kx\in K and +∞+\infty otherwise. The Legendre transform of φ:ℝn→ℝ\varphi\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is given by ℒ​φ​(x)=supy∈ℝn(⟨x,y⟩−φ⁡(x)){\cal L}\varphi(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}(\langle x,y\rangle-\varphi(x)). Finally, the inf convolution of two functions f,g:ℝn→ℝf,g\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is defined by (f​□​g)​(z)=infx+y=z{f⁡(x)+g⁡(y)}(f\square g)(z)=\inf_{x+y=z}\left\{f(x)+g(y)\right\}.

Organization of the paper: In Section 2 we prove Theorem 1.3. In Section 3 we prove Theorem 1.8 and its consequence, Theorem 1.9. In Section 4 we discuss the planar case of Conjecture 1.2. Finally, in the appendix, we give for completeness another proof of Theorem 1.6, which is more geometric in nature, and follows Rogers and Shephard’s arguments from [12].

2 Proof of Theorem 1.3

In this section we prove Theorem 1.3. We start with the following lemma regarding the volume of the convex hull of homothetic copies of a simplex SS and of −S-S, which is the expression appearing in Conjecture 1.2.

Lemma 2.1.

Let S⊂ℝnS\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a centered simplex. For λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that (n+1)​(1−λ)−1≤k≤(n+1)​(1−λ)(n+1)(1-\lambda)-1\leq k\leq(n+1)(1-\lambda). Then

Vol⁡((1−λ)​S∨(−λ​S))Vol⁡(S)=(nk)​(1−λ)k​λn−k.\frac{{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)S\vee(-\lambda S))}{{\rm Vol}(S)}=\binom{n}{k}(1-\lambda)^{k}\lambda^{n-k}. (9)
Remark 2.2.

Usually, the above inequality determines k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda) uniquely. When it does not (i.e. there are two such kk’s), the corresponding expressions on the right hand side of (9) coincide.

Proof of Lemma 2.1.

Note first that by symmetry, it is enough to assume that λ≤12\lambda\leq{\frac{1}{2}}. Moreover, since SS is centered, for λ≤1n+1\lambda\leq{\frac{1}{n+1}} one has −λ​S⊆(1−λ)​S-\lambda S\subseteq(1-\lambda)S (see [1], page 57), and hence (9)(\ref{formula-conv-simplices}) holds trivially. Thus, we can further assume that 1n+1≤λ{\frac{1}{n+1}}\leq\lambda. Next, since

Vol⁡((1−λ)​S∨(−λ​S))=(1−λ)n​Vol​(S∨(−λ1−λ​S)),{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)S\vee(-\lambda S))=(1-\lambda)^{n}{\rm Vol}(S\vee(-\tfrac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}S)), (10)

it is enough to compute the quantity Vol⁡(S∨(−t​S))Vol⁡(S)\frac{{\rm Vol}(S\vee(-tS))}{{\rm Vol}(S)} for t=λ1−λt=\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}. In these notations, our assumptions become t∈[1n,1]t\in[\tfrac{1}{n},1] and n+11+t−1≤k≤n+11+t\frac{n+1}{1+t}-1\leq k\leq\frac{n+1}{1+t}. Moreover, for simplicity, we may take SS to be the convex hull of {ej}j=1n+1\{e_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n+1} (vectors of the standard basis of ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}) embedded in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, which has a=(1n+1,…,1n+1)a=(\frac{1}{n+1},\dots,\frac{1}{n+1}) as its center of mass. We then wish to compute the nn-dimensional volume of Kt:=S∨StK_{t}:=S\vee S_{t}, with StS_{t} being the convex hull of the vectors vj=(1+t)​a−t​ejv_{j}=(1+t)a-te_{j}, where j=1,…,n+1j=1,\dots,n+1.

First, we study the facets of KtK_{t}. Consider Fk=conv⁡{e1,…,ek,vk+1,…,vn}F_{k}={\rm conv}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{k},v_{k+1},\dots,v_{n}\}, for some k∈{1,…​n}k\in\{1,\dots n\}. Note that FkF_{k} lies in the intersection of the two hyperplanes a+a⟂a+a^{\perp} and e1+(uk)⟂e_{1}+(u_{k})^{\perp}, where

uk=(−t,…,−t⏟k​ times,1,…,1⏟n−k​ times,(1+t)​k−n).u_{k}=\Bigl(\underset{k\text{ times}}{\underbrace{-t,\dots,-t}},\underset{n-k\text{ times}}{\underbrace{1,\dots,1}},\left(1+t\right)k-n\Bigr).

For FkF_{k} to be a facet of KtK_{t}, we require that for all j=1,…,n+1j=1,\dots,n+1, one has ⟨ej,uk⟩≥−t\langle e_{j},u_{k}\rangle\geq-t, ⟨vj,uk⟩≥−t\langle v_{j},u_{k}\rangle\geq-t, and that ⟨uk,ν⟩=−t\langle u_{k},\nu\rangle=-t only for ν\nu which is a vertex of FkF_{k}. A direct computation shows that this holds if and only if n+11+t−1<k<n+11+t\frac{n+1}{1+t}-1<k<\frac{n+1}{1+t}. Note that for all jj, eje_{j} and vjv_{j} never participate in the same facet, and hence every facet of KtK_{t} consists of either nn or n+1n+1 vertices. By Remark 2.3 below, we may assume that every facet of KtK_{t} is of the form of FkF_{k}, i.e., consists of exactly nn vertices, kk of which are vertices of SS.

The contribution of Fk∨{a}F_{k}\vee\{a\} to the ratio Vol⁡(Kt)Vol⁡(S)\frac{{\rm Vol}(K_{t})}{{\rm Vol}(S)} can be easily computed by noticing that, by invariance under translation, Voln​(Fk∨{a})=Voln​(V){\rm Vol}_{n}(F_{k}\vee\{a\})={\rm Vol}_{n}(V), where

V=conv⁡{0,e1−a,…,ek−a,−t⁡(ek+1−a),…,−t⁡(en−a)}.V={\rm conv}\{0,e_{1}-a,\dots,e_{k}-a,-t(e_{k+1}-a),\dots,-t(e_{n}-a)\}.

Moreover, since

Voln​(V)​|a|n+1\displaystyle\frac{{\rm Vol}_{n}(V)|a|}{n+1} =\displaystyle= Voln+1​(conv⁡{0,e1−a,…,ek−a,−t⁡(ek+1−a),…,−t⁡(en−a),a})\displaystyle{\rm Vol}_{n+1}({\rm conv}\{0,e_{1}-a,\dots,e_{k}-a,-t(e_{k+1}-a),\dots,-t(e_{n}-a),a\})
=\displaystyle= tn−k​Voln+1​(conv⁡{0,e1−a,…,ek−a,ek+1−a,…,en−a,a}),\displaystyle t^{n-k}{\rm Vol}_{n+1}({\rm conv}\{0,e_{1}-a,\dots,e_{k}-a,e_{k+1}-a,\dots,e_{n}-a,a\}),

and 1n+1​Voln​(S)​|a|=Voln+1​(conv⁡{0,e1,…,en+1})\frac{1}{n+1}{\rm Vol}_{n}(S)|a|={\rm Vol}_{n+1}({\rm conv}\{0,e_{1},\dots,e_{n+1}\}), one has

Voln​(Fk∨{a})Voln​S=tn−k​det(e1−a,…,en−a,a)=tn−kn+1.\frac{{\rm Vol}_{n}(F_{k}\vee\{a\})}{{\rm Vol}_{n}S}=t^{n-k}\det(e_{1}-a,\dots,e_{n}-a,a)=\frac{t^{n-k}}{n+1}.

Finally, summing over all of the facets of KtK_{t}, we get

Vol⁡(Kt)Vol⁡(S)=(n+1)​(nk)​tn−k​1n+1=(nk)​tn−k,\frac{{\rm Vol}(K_{t})}{{\rm Vol}(S)}=(n+1)\binom{n}{k}t^{n-k}\frac{1}{n+1}=\binom{n}{k}t^{n-k},

which by the definition of tt and (10), gives the desired result. ∎

Remark 2.3.

Unless t=n+1−jjt=\frac{n+1-j}{j} (equivalently, λ=n+1−jn+1\lambda=\frac{n+1-j}{n+1}), for some j∈{[n2],…,n}j\in\{[\frac{n}{2}],\dots,n\}, the value of kk (which is now uniquely determined) satisfies the strict inequality n+11+t−1<k<n+11+t\frac{n+1}{1+t}-1<k<\frac{n+1}{1+t}. Thus, in this case, for FkF_{k} to be a facet of KtK_{t} it must be the convex hull of nn vertices. From continuity of the resulting volume ratio formula, it suffices to handle this case only, as done in the proof of Lemma 2.1.

We are now in a position to prove Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} be a convex body, and assume that Conjecture 1.2 holds. We wish to show that Conjecture 1.1 holds as well. Note that our assumption is that for every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] there exists x∈Kx\in K such that

Vol⁡((1−λ)​(K−x)∨λ⁡(x−K))Vol⁡(K)≤Vol⁡((1−λ)​S∨−λ​S)Vol⁡(S),\frac{{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)(K-x)\vee\lambda(x-K))}{{\rm Vol}(K)}\leq\frac{{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)S\vee-\lambda S)}{{\rm Vol}(S)},

where SS is a centered simplex. Using the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.4, the monotonicity, homogeneity in each argument, and translation invariance of the mixed volume yield, for every λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1):

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])Vol⁡(K)≤Vol⁡((1−λ)​(K−x)∨λ⁡(x−K))(1−λ)j​λn−j​Vol​(K).\frac{V(K[j],-K[n-j])}{{\rm Vol}(K)}\leq\frac{{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)(K-x)\vee\lambda(x-K))}{(1-\lambda)^{j}\lambda^{n-j}{\rm Vol}(K)}.

We may then use Lemma 2.1 with k=jk=j and λ=n+1−jn+1∈(0,1)\lambda=\frac{n+1-j}{n+1}\in(0,1), together with the last two inequalities, to get

V⁡(K⁡[j],−K⁡[n−j])Vol⁡(K)≤Vol⁡((1−λ)​S∨−λ​S)(1−λ)j​λn−j​Vol​(S)=(nj).\frac{V(K[j],-K[n-j])}{{\rm Vol}(K)}\leq\frac{{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)S\vee-\lambda S)}{(1-\lambda)^{j}\lambda^{n-j}{\rm Vol}(S)}=\binom{n}{j}.

This completes the proof of Theorem 1.3. ∎

Remark 2.4.

Note that in the above proof we apply Conjecture 1.2 only for finitely many values of the parameter λ\lambda.

3 The λ\lambda-difference function

In [3], Colesanti introduced the so called “difference function”, which is a functional analogue of the difference body notion. He then proved a functional version of the difference body inequality (1) and used it to provide yet another proof of (6)(\ref{RS-ineq-conv-hull}). In this section, we generalize Colesanti’s definition and, using similar methods, extend the main result of [3].

First, we recall our notion of a λ\lambda-difference function (Definition 1.7). For two functions f,g:ℝn→ℝ+f,g:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}, and λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), the λ\lambda-difference function Δλf,g\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g} of ff and gg is

Δλf,g​(z)=sup(1−λ)​x+λ​y=zf1−λ​(x1−λ)​gλ​(−yλ).\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}(z)=\sup_{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y=z}f^{1-\lambda}\left(\tfrac{x}{1-\lambda}\right)g^{\lambda}\left({\tfrac{-y}{\lambda}}\right).

Alternatively if f=e−φ,g=e−ψf=e^{-\varphi},\,g=e^{-\psi} we may write

Δλf,g=e−δλφ,ψ,whereδλφ,ψ​(z)=inf(1−λ)​x+λ​y=z{(1−λ)​φ​(x1−λ)+λ​ψ​(−yλ)}.\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}=e^{-\delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}},\ {\rm where}\ \ \delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}(z)=\inf_{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y=z}\left\{(1-\lambda)\varphi(\tfrac{x}{1-\lambda})+\lambda\psi(\tfrac{-y}{\lambda})\right\}.
Remark 3.1.

1) The λ\lambda-difference function is compatible with translations, and multiplications by positive constants. More precisely, denoting fa​(x):=f⁡(x+a)f_{a}(x):=f(x+a), one has Δλfa,gb=(Δλf,g)(1−λ)​a+λ​b\Delta_{\lambda}^{f_{a},g_{b}}=(\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g})_{(1-\lambda)a+\lambda b}\, and Δλa​f,b​g=a1−λ​bλ​Δλf,g\Delta_{\lambda}^{af,bg}=a^{1-\lambda}b^{\lambda}\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}.

2) Letting Φ⁡(x)=φ⁡(x/(1−λ))\varPhi(x)=\varphi(x/(1-\lambda)), Ψ(x)=ψ(−x/λ)\Psi(x)=\psi(-x/\lambda), we may apply the Prékopa-Leindler inequality for the functions e−Φ,e−Ψe^{-\varPhi},e^{-\Psi}, and e−δλφ,ψe^{-{\delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}}}, and obtain the following estimate:

∫ℝnΔλf,g≥((1−λ)1−λ​λλ)n​(∫ℝnf)1−λ​(∫ℝng)λ.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}\geq\left((1-\lambda)^{1-\lambda}\lambda^{\lambda}\right)^{n}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f\right)^{1-\lambda}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\right)^{\lambda}.

Theorem 1.8, which we now turn to prove, gives a complementary upper bound.

Proof of Theorem 1.8:

Assume that f=e−φ,g=e−ψf=e^{-\varphi},\,g=e^{-\psi}, for some convex functions φ,ψ\varphi,\,\psi. Let z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. First, assume that there exist x∗,y∗∈ℝnx^{*},y^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

(1−λ)x∗+λy∗=z,andδλφ,ψ(z)=(1−λ)φ(x∗/(1−λ))+λψ(−y∗/λ).(1-\lambda)x^{*}+\lambda y^{*}=z,\ {\rm and}\ \ \delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}(z)=(1-\lambda)\varphi(x^{*}/(1-\lambda))+\lambda\psi(-y^{*}/\lambda).

Using the convexity of φ\varphi and ψ\psi, for every y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n} one has

ψ((1−λ)y−z/λ)≤(1−λ)ψ(y−x∗/λ))+λψ(−y∗/λ),\psi\left((1-\lambda)y-z/\lambda\right)\leq(1-\lambda)\psi(y-x^{*}/\lambda))+\lambda\psi(-y^{*}/\lambda),

and

φ⁡(λ​y)≤(1−λ)​φ​(x∗/(1−λ))+λ​φ​(y−x∗/λ).\varphi\left(\lambda y\right)\leq(1-\lambda)\varphi(x^{*}/(1-\lambda))+\lambda\varphi(y-x^{*}/\lambda).

Summing these two inequalities, we obtain

ψ⁡((1−λ)​y−z/λ)+φ⁡(λ​y)≤δλφ,ψ​(z)+λ​φ​(y−x∗/λ)+(1−λ)​ψ​(y−x∗/λ).\psi\left((1-\lambda)y-z/\lambda\right)+\varphi\left(\lambda y\right)\leq\delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}(z)+\lambda\varphi(y-x^{*}/\lambda)+(1-\lambda)\psi(y-x^{*}/\lambda). (11)

As this holds for every y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we integrate (11)(\ref{eq-twice-convexity}) over y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and obtain

Δλf,g​(z)​∫ℝnfλ​g1−λ≤∫ℝng⁡((1−λ)​y−z/λ)​f​(λ​y)​𝑑y.\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g}(z)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f^{\lambda}g^{1-\lambda}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\left((1-\lambda)y-z/\lambda\right)f\left(\lambda y\right)dy. (12)

If the case where the infimum in the definition of δλφ,ψ​(z)\delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}(z) is not attained, there are sequences (xj)j=1∞,(yj)j=1∞⊂ℝn(x_{j})_{j=1}^{\infty},(y_{j})_{j=1}^{\infty}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} such that for every jj, (1−λ)​xj+λ​yj=z(1-\lambda)x_{j}+\lambda y_{j}=z, and δλφ,ψ(z)=limj→∞((1−λ)φ(xj/(1−λ))+λφ(−yj/λ))\delta_{\lambda}^{\varphi,\psi}(z)=\lim_{j\to\infty}((1-\lambda)\varphi(x_{j}/(1-\lambda))+\lambda\varphi(-y_{j}/\lambda)). Using the same argument as before, one has,

f1−λ(xj/(1−λ))gλ(−yj/λ)∫ℝnfλg1−λ≤∫ℝng((1−λ)y−z/λ)f(λy)dy,f^{1-\lambda}(x_{j}/(1-\lambda))g^{\lambda}(-y_{j}/\lambda)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f^{\lambda}g^{1-\lambda}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\left((1-\lambda)y-z/\lambda\right)f\left(\lambda y\right)dy,

and by taking the limit we get that (12) holds in this case as well. We may therefore integrate this inequality with respect to z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and get

∫ℝnfλ​g1−λ​∫ℝnΔλf,g\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f^{\lambda}g^{1-\lambda}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\Delta_{\lambda}^{f,g} ≤∫ℝn(∫ℝng⁡((1−λ)​y−z/λ)​f​(λ​y)​𝑑y)​𝑑z\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\left((1-\lambda)y-z/\lambda\right)f\left(\lambda y\right)dy\right)dz
=∫ℝnf⁡(λ​y)​(∫ℝng⁡((1−λ)​y−z/λ)​𝑑z)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f\left(\lambda y\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\left((1-\lambda)y-z/\lambda\right)dz\right)dy
=∫ℝnf(λy)dy∫ℝng(−z/λ)dz\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f\left(\lambda y\right)dy\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\left(-z/\lambda\right)dz
=(∫ℝnf)​(∫ℝng).\displaystyle=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g\right).

This completes the proof of Theorem 1.8. ∎

Remark 3.2.

For λ=1/2\lambda=1/2 and f=gf=g, Colesanti showed in [3] that the bound (8)(\ref{lambda-difference-function-theorem}) is sharp and attained for the function

g⁡(x)={e−(x1+⋯+xn),if xj≥0,∀j=1,…,n0,otherwise.g(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-(x_{1}+\dots+x_{n})},&\text{if }x_{j}\geq 0,\quad\forall j=1,\dots,n\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

In fact, this function shows that the bound is sharp for every λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1). Indeed, one can easily verify that Δλg,g(z)=e−∑i=1n|zj|λ\Delta_{\lambda}^{g,g}(z)=e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}|z_{j}|_{\lambda}}, where

|a|λ={|a|1−λ,if ​a≥0|a|λ,otherwise.|a|_{\lambda}=\begin{cases}\frac{|a|}{1-\lambda},&\text{if }a\geq 0\\ \frac{|a|}{\lambda},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Thus, a direct computation gives

∫ℝnΔλg,g(z)dz=∫ℝne−∑|zj|λdz=∑j=0n(nj)λj(1−λ)n−j(∫0∞e−xdx)n=1=∫ℝng.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\Delta_{\lambda}^{g,g}(z)dz=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-\sum|z_{j}|_{\lambda}}dz=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\lambda^{j}(1-\lambda)^{n-j}\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x}dx\right)^{n}=1=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g.

Theorem 1.8 provides, as an immediate corollary, a proof of Theorem 1.9.

Proof of Theorem 1.9.

Let K,L⊆ℝnK,L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be two convex bodies, and without loss of generality assume they contain the origin. Let λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1). Using the homogeneity of the support function hK∘​(x)h_{K^{\circ}}(x) (both in KK and in xx), one has

δλhK∘,hL∘(z)=inf(1−λ)​x+λ​y=z((1−λ)hK∘(x/(1−λ))+λhL∘(−y/λ))=h11−λ​K∘□h−1λ​L∘(z),\delta_{\lambda}^{h_{K^{\circ}},h_{L^{\circ}}}(z)=\inf_{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y=z}((1-\lambda)h_{K^{\circ}}(x/(1-\lambda))+\lambda h_{L^{\circ}}(-y/\lambda))=h_{\frac{1}{1-\lambda}K^{\circ}}\Box h_{-\frac{1}{\lambda}L^{\circ}}(z),

where f​□​gf\Box g is the infimal convolution of ff and gg. It is well known (see e.g., [14], Section 1.7), that for lower semi continuous convex functions f,gf,g we have f​□​g=ℒ⁡(ℒ​f+ℒ​g)f\Box g={\cal L}({\cal L}f+{\cal L}g) and that ℒ​hK=1K∞{\cal L}h_{K}=\textbf{1}_{K}^{\infty}. Thus,

δλhK∘,hL∘=ℒ⁡(111−λ​K∘∞+1−1λ​L∘∞)=ℒ⁡(111−λ​K∘∩−1λ​L∘∞)=h11−λ​K∘∩−1λ​L∘=h((1−λ)​K∨−λ​L)∘.\begin{split}\delta_{\lambda}^{h_{K^{\circ}},h_{L^{\circ}}}&={\cal L}(\textbf{1}_{\frac{1}{1-\lambda}K^{\circ}}^{\infty}+\textbf{1}_{-\frac{1}{\lambda}L^{\circ}}^{\infty})={\cal L}(\textbf{1}_{\frac{1}{1-\lambda}K^{\circ}\cap-\frac{1}{\lambda}L^{\circ}}^{\infty})\\ &=h_{\frac{1}{1-\lambda}K^{\circ}\cap-\frac{1}{\lambda}L^{\circ}}=h_{((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda L)^{\circ}}.\end{split}

Moreover, note that (e−hK∘)λ​(e−hL∘)1−λ=e−hλ​K∘+(1−λ)​L∘(e^{-h_{K^{\circ}}})^{\lambda}(e^{-h_{L^{\circ}}})^{1-\lambda}=e^{-h_{\lambda K^{\circ}+(1-\lambda)L^{\circ}}}. Thus, combining the fact that ∫ℝne−hK∘=n!​Vol​(K)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{-h_{K^{\circ}}}=n!{\rm Vol}(K) with Theorem 1.8 for f=e−hK∘f=e^{-h_{K^{\circ}}} and g=e−hL∘,g=e^{-h_{L^{\circ}}}, yields

Vol⁡((1−λ)​K∨−λ​L)​Vol​((λ​K∘+(1−λ)​L∘)∘)≤Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L),{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda L)\,{\rm Vol}((\lambda K^{\circ}+(1-\lambda)L^{\circ})^{\circ})\leq{\rm Vol}(K)\,{\rm Vol}(L),

or, equivalently,

Vol⁡(K∨−L)​Vol​((K∘+L∘)∘)≤Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L).{\rm Vol}(K\vee-L)\,{\rm Vol}((K^{\circ}+L^{\circ})^{\circ})\leq{\rm Vol}(K)\,{\rm Vol}(L).

The proof of Theorem 1.9 is thus complete. ∎

4 The planar case

While Godbersen’s conjecture is clearly true for n=2n=2 by the inclusion −K⊂2​K-K\subset 2K for centered convex regions in the plane, the validity of the other two conjectures presented in Section 1 is not as self-evident. In this section we assert the validity of Conjecture 1.2 when n=2n=2. We note that in the plane, the case λ=12\lambda=\frac{1}{2} (along with a characterization of the equality case) was first established by Estermann [5], and later by Levi [10], Fáry [7] and Yaglom and Boltyanskiĭ [16]. We refer the reader to [4] for a detailed survey, which contains not only the history of these problems and several proofs, but also similar related problems dealing with intersections of the convex bodies KK and −t​K-tK.

We show that Conjecture 1.2 holds in the plane (for every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]):

Theorem 4.1.

Let K⊆ℝ2K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2} be a convex body, and let λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. If xx is the center of mass of KK, then

Area⁡((1−λ)​(K−x)∨λ⁡(x−K))≤Area⁡((1−λ)​S∨−λ​S),{\rm Area}((1-\lambda)(K-x)\vee\lambda(x-K))\leq{\rm Area}((1-\lambda)S\vee-\lambda S),

where SS is a centered triangle such that Area⁡(K)=Area⁡(S){\rm Area}(K)={\rm Area}(S).

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Without loss of generality, we may assume that KK is centered and has unit area, and show that

Area⁡((1−λ)​K∨−λ​K)≤Area⁡((1−λ)​S∨−λ​S).{\rm Area}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K)\leq{\rm Area}((1-\lambda)S\vee-\lambda S).

We may further assume that KK is a polygon, and by a standard continuity argument, the result will hold for a general convex body.

We will describe an inductive process, in which we remove the vertices of KK one by one until reaching a triangle. In each step, we replace the body KK with a body K′K^{\prime} which has one vertex less, without changing the area or the center of mass, and without decreasing the area of (1−λ)​K∨−λ​K(1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K. Let K=Conv⁡{x1,…,xN}K={\rm Conv}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\}, where N≥4N\geq 4. For t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, consider the body

K~t=Conv⁡{x1,x2+t​u,x3,…,xN},with​u=x3−x1.\widetilde{K}_{t}={\rm Conv}\{x_{1},x_{2}+tu,x_{3},\ldots,x_{N}\},\ {\rm with}\ u=x_{3}-x_{1}.

Denote by l1l_{1} and l3l_{3} the lines containing the segments [xN,x1][x_{N},x_{1}] and [x3,x4][x_{3},x_{4}] respectively. Let α<0<β\alpha<0<\beta be such that x2+α​u∈l1x_{2}+\alpha u\in l_{1}, and x2+β​u∈l3x_{2}+\beta u\in l_{3}. Note that for t∈[α,β]t\in[\alpha,\beta] one has K~t=Conv⁡{x1,x3,…,xN}∪Conv⁡{x1,x2+t​u,x3}\widetilde{K}_{t}={\rm Conv}\{x_{1},x_{3},\ldots,x_{N}\}\cup{\rm Conv}\{x_{1},x_{2}+tu,x_{3}\}, and thus Area⁡(K~t)=Area⁡(K){\rm Area}(\widetilde{K}_{t})={\rm Area}(K). Moreover, the center of mass of K~t\widetilde{K}_{t} is θ​t​u\theta tu, where θ=13​Area​(Conv⁡{x1,x2,x3})\theta=\frac{1}{3}{\rm Area}({\rm Conv}\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}). Indeed, the center of mass of a union of two planar sets is the average of the centers of mass, weighted by their respective areas. Denote Kt=K~t−θ​t​uK_{t}=\widetilde{K}_{t}-\theta tu. Note that for t∈[α,β]t\in[\alpha,\beta], KtK_{t} has its center of mass at the origin, and Area⁡(Kt)=Area⁡(K)=1{\rm Area}(K_{t})={\rm Area}(K)=1.

The family of bodies {(1−λ)​Kt∨−λ​Kt}t∈[α,β]\{(1-\lambda)K_{t}\vee-\lambda K_{t}\}_{t\in[\alpha,\beta]} is a linear parameter system (see [13] for the definition), since all vertices are moving parallel to uu. Therefore the area of (1−λ)​Kt∨−λ​Kt(1-\lambda)K_{t}\vee-\lambda K_{t} is a convex function of tt, and attains its maximum in one of the edges of the interval [α,β][\alpha,\beta]. Assume the maximum is achieved at α\alpha, and set K′=KαK^{\prime}=K_{\alpha}. Then, in addition to having unit area and center of mass at the origin, K′K^{\prime} satisfies

Area⁡((1−λ)​K∨−λ​K)≤Area⁡((1−λ)​K′∨−λ​K′),{\rm Area}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K)\leq{\rm Area}((1-\lambda)K^{\prime}\vee-\lambda K^{\prime}),

as K=K0K=K_{0}. Since x2+α​u∈l1x_{2}+\alpha u\in l_{1}, K′K^{\prime} has one less vertex than KK, and thus the proof is complete. ∎

5 Appendix

We give here another proof of Theorem 1.6. The proof is attained by essentially repeating the arguments from [12], but instead of considering KK and −K-K, we consider two general convex bodies KK and LL. Moreover, we will be able to characterize the equality case in Theorem 1.5.

5.1 The Rogers–Shephard body

We consider the following (2​n+1)(2n+1)-dimensional body (see Figure 2), a special case of which, where K=LK=L, plays a central role in [12].

G(K,L):={(x,y,θ)∈ℝn×ℝn×ℝ|θ∈[0,1],x∈θK,x+y∈(1−θ)L}.G{(K,L)}:=\left\{\left(x,y,\theta\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}\,|\,\theta\in\left[0,1\right],\,x\in\theta K,\,x+y\in(1-\theta)L\right\}.

The projection of G⁡(K,L)G{(K,L)} onto the (n+1)\left(n+1\right)-dimensional subspace of points of the form (0,y,θ)\left(0,y,\theta\right) is denoted by C(K,L)={(0,y,θ)|θ∈[0,1],y∈(1−θ)L−θK}C(K,L)=\{(0,y,\theta)\ |\ \theta\in[0,1],\ y\in(1-\theta)L-\theta K\}. Equivalently,

C(K,L)={0}×conv(L×{0},−K×{1})⊆{0}×ℝn+1.C(K,L)=\{0\}\times{\rm conv}\left(L\times\left\{0\right\},\,-K\times\left\{1\right\}\right)\subseteq\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. (13)

When K=LK=L, this is exactly the body C⁡(K)C(K) used in [12].

The main tool used by Rogers and Shephard in [12] for finding an upper bound for the volume of the difference body is the following theorem which we provide along with its proof, for the convenience of the reader.

Theorem 5.1 (Rogers and Shephard).

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body, and let H=K∩EH=K\cap E be a jj-dimensional section of KK, and LL the orthogonal projection of KK onto E⟂E^{\perp}. Then

j!​(n−j)!n!​Volj​(H)​Voln−j​(L)≤Voln​(K).\frac{j!\left(n-j\right)!}{n!}{\rm Vol}_{j}\left(H\right){\rm Vol}_{n-j}\left(L\right)\leq{\rm Vol}_{n}\left(K\right). (14)

Moreover, equality holds if and only if for every direction v∈E⟂v\in E^{\perp}, the intersection of KK with E+ℝ+​vE+\mathbb{R}^{+}v is obtained by taking the convex hull of HH and one more point.

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

The proof consists of two arguments. The first one is that all of the quantities in (14) are invariant under a Schwarz symmetrization, so we may assume that all intersections of KK parallel to HH are (centered) dilates of a ball. That is, we may consider the body:

K∗={(l,y)∈ℝn−j×ℝj|l∈L,|y|≤(Volj​(Kl)Volj​(B2j))1/j},K^{*}=\left\{(l,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-j}\times\mathbb{R}^{j}\quad|\quad l\in L,\ |y|\leq\left(\frac{{\rm Vol}_{j}(K_{l})}{{\rm Vol}_{j}(B_{2}^{j})}\right)^{1/j}\right\},

where Kl=K∩(E+l)K_{l}=K\cap(E+l), for every l∈Ll\in L. Their second argument is that H∗∨L⊆K∗H^{*}\vee L\subseteq K^{*}, where H∗H^{*} denotes the section K∗∩EK^{*}\cap E. Then, a simple computation shows that the left-hand side of (14) equals Voln​(H∗∨L){\rm Vol}_{n}(H^{*}\vee L), and thus inequality (14) holds.

Assume now that equality holds in (14). First note that H∗∨L⊆K∗H^{*}\vee L\subseteq K^{*}, thus equality in volumes implies K∗=H∗∨L=H∗∨∂LK^{*}=H^{*}\vee L=H^{*}\vee\partial L. Moreover, for every direction v∈E⟂v\in E^{\perp}, let [0,l]=L∩(ℝ+​v)[0,l]=L\cap(\mathbb{R}^{+}v), and for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], let fv​(t)=Volj​(Kt​l)1/jf_{v}(t)={\rm Vol}_{j}(K_{tl})^{1/j}. Note that fvf_{v} is invariant under Schwartz symmetrization, hence for every v∈E⟂v\in E^{\perp}, fvf_{v} is linear, and fv​(1)=0f_{v}(1)=0. Since Kt​lK_{tl} contains t​Kl+(1−t)​HtK_{l}+(1-t)H, from Brunn Minkowski’s inequality one has

fv​(t)=Volj​(Kt​l)1/j≥t​Volj​(Kl)1/j+(1−t)​Volj​(H)1/j=(1−t)​fv​(0).f_{v}(t)={\rm Vol}_{j}(K_{tl})^{1/j}\geq t{\rm Vol}_{j}(K_{l})^{1/j}+(1-t){\rm Vol}_{j}(H)^{1/j}=(1-t)f_{v}(0).

Thus, from the equality case in Brunn Minkowski’s inequality, KlK_{l} is a homothety of HH of zero volume, i.e. it is a point. Moreover, for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one has Kt​l=t​Kl+(1−t)​HK_{tl}=tK_{l}+(1-t)H, and thus K∩(E+ℝ+​v)=H∨KlK\cap(E+\mathbb{R}^{+}v)=H\vee K_{l}, and the proof is complete. ∎

5.2 An upper bound for the volume of C⁡(K,L)C(K,L)

Theorem 5.2.

For convex bodies K,L⊆ℝnK,L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, let C⁡(K,L)C(K,L) be as defined in (13). For every θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1],

Voln+1​(C⁡(K,L))≤1n+1​(Voln​(K)​Voln​(L)Voln​(θ​K∩(1−θ)​L)).{\rm Vol}_{n+1}\left(C\left(K,L\right)\right)\leq\frac{1}{n+1}\left(\frac{{\rm Vol}_{n}\left(K\right){\rm Vol}_{n}\left(L\right)}{{\rm Vol}_{n}(\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L)}\right).

In [12] this bound was obtained for the specific case K=LK=L and θ=12\theta=\frac{1}{2}.

Proof of Theorem 5.2.

In order to estimate Voln+1​(C​(K,L)){\rm Vol}_{n+1}\left(C\left(K,L\right)\right), we apply Theorem 5.1 for the body G⁡(K,L)G{(K,L)}, and the nn-dimensional affine subspace E={θ=θ0,y=0}E=\{\theta=\theta_{0},y=0\}. First, by Fubini’s Theorem,

Vol2​n+1​(G​(K,L))\displaystyle{\rm Vol}_{2n+1}\left(G{(K,L)}\right) =\displaystyle= ∫01d​θ​∫θ​KVoln​((1−θ)​L)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}d\theta\int_{\theta K}{\rm Vol}_{n}((1-\theta)L)dx
=\displaystyle= Voln​(K)​Voln​(L)​∫01θn​(1−θ)n​𝑑θ\displaystyle{\rm Vol}_{n}\left(K\right){\rm Vol}_{n}\left(L\right)\int_{0}^{1}\theta^{n}\left(1-\theta\right)^{n}d\theta
=\displaystyle= Voln​(K)​Voln​(L)​n!​n!(2​n+1)!.\displaystyle{\rm Vol}_{n}\left(K\right){\rm Vol}_{n}\left(L\right)\frac{n!n!}{\left(2n+1\right)!}.

As in Theorem 5.1, set H=G⁡(K,L)∩EH=G{(K,L)}\cap E. Note that Voln​(H)=Voln​(θ0​K∩(1−θ0)​L){\rm Vol}_{n}(H)={\rm Vol}_{n}(\theta_{0}K\cap(1-\theta_{0})L). As mentioned before, the projection of G⁡(K,L)G{(K,L)} on E⟂E^{\perp} is exactly C⁡(K,L)C\left(K,L\right), and using Theorem 5.1 we get

n!​(n+1)!(2​n+1)!​Voln+1​(C⁡(K,L))​Voln​(θ0​K∩(1−θ0)​L)≤Vol2​n+1​(G⁡(K,L)).\frac{n!\left(n+1\right)!}{\left(2n+1\right)!}{\rm Vol}_{n+1}\left(C\left(K,L\right)\right){\rm Vol}_{n}\left(\theta_{0}K\cap(1-\theta_{0})L\right)\leq{\rm Vol}_{2n+1}\left(G{(K,L)}\right). (15)

Plugging in the volume of G⁡(K,L)G{(K,L)} completes the proof of the theorem. ∎

5.3 A second proof of Theorem 1.6

Using Theorem 5.1, this time for the body C⁡(K,L)C(K,L), and the volume bound from Theorem 5.2, we can give yet another proof of Theorem 1.6.

Proof of Theorem 1.6.

Let K,L⊆ℝnK,L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be two convex bodies such that 0∈K∩L0\in K\cap L, and set θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1]. We need to show that

Vol⁡(L∨−K)​Vol​(θ​K∩(1−θ)​L)≤Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L).{\rm Vol}(L\vee-K)\,{\rm Vol}(\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L)\leq{\rm Vol}(K){\rm Vol}(L).

Let EE be the 1-dimensional subspace of ℝn+1{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} given by E={x=0}E=\{x=0\}. The body L∨−KL\vee-K is the nn-dimensional projection of C⁡(K,L)C(K,L) onto the subspace E⟂={(x,0)|x∈ℝn}E^{\perp}=\{(x,0)\,|\,x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}. Since 0∈K∩L0\in K\cap L, the section H=E∩C⁡(K,L)H=E\cap C(K,L) is a unit segment. By Theorem 5.1,

1n+1​Voln​(−K∨L)≤Voln+1​(C⁡(K,L)).\frac{1}{n+1}{\rm Vol}_{n}(-K\vee L)\leq{\rm Vol}_{n+1}(C(K,L)). (16)

Combining this with the volume bound for C⁡(K,L)C(K,L) established in Theorem 5.2 above, we get the desired inequality. ∎

5.4 The equality case in Theorem 1.5 and in Theorem 1.6

Here we characterize the equality cases in Theorems 1.5 and 1.6. We start with the former, and show that equality holds in (7)(\ref{ineq-needed-for-God}) if and only if KK is a simplex with a vertex at the origin. Indeed, it is not hard to check that for the standard simplex SS one has

Vol⁡((1−λ)​S∨−λ​S)=∑k=0n(nk)​(1−λ)k​λn−k​Vol​(S)=Vol⁡(S).{\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)S\vee-\lambda S)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(1-\lambda)^{k}\lambda^{n-k}{\rm Vol}(S)={\rm Vol}(S).

As for the other direction, assume that Vol⁡((1−λ)​K∨−λ​K)=Vol⁡(K){\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K)={\rm Vol}(K). We wish to show that KK is a simplex with 00 as one of its vertices. Recall from the introduction that Theorem 1.6, for (1−λ)​K,λ​K(1-\lambda)K,\lambda K, and θ0=λ\theta_{0}=\lambda, immediately yields inequality (7)(\ref{ineq-needed-for-God}). Combining (15) and (16) in this case yields

Voln​(−(1−λ)​K∨λ​K)≤(n+1)​Voln+1​(C⁡((1−λ)​K,λ​K))≤Voln​(K).{\rm Vol}_{n}(-(1-\lambda)K\vee\lambda K)\leq(n+1){\rm Vol}_{n+1}(C((1-\lambda)K,\lambda K))\leq{\rm Vol}_{n}(K). (17)

From the assumption Vol⁡((1−λ)​K∨−λ​K)=Vol⁡(K){\rm Vol}((1-\lambda)K\vee-\lambda K)={\rm Vol}(K) it follows that both inequalities in (17)(\ref{eq:C-versus-(aK-V-(x-bK))}) are in fact equalities. In particular, equality holds in (15) for the bodies (1−λ)​K,λ​K(1-\lambda)K,\lambda K, and θ0=λ\theta_{0}=\lambda. By the equality condition in Theorem 5.1, this implies in particular that sections of the body G⁡((1−λ)​K,λ​K)G{((1-\lambda)K,\lambda K)} by affine subspaces of the form {(x,y,θ)|x∈ℝn,y=y0,θ=λ}\{(x,y,\theta)|x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},y=y_{0},\theta=\lambda\}, for any y0∈λ⁡(1−λ)​K−λ⁡(1−λ)​Ky_{0}\in\lambda(1-\lambda)K-\lambda(1-\lambda)K (which are given by λ⁡(1−λ)​K∩λ⁡(1−λ)​K−y0\lambda(1-\lambda)K\cap\lambda(1-\lambda)K-y_{0}), are homothetic. Thus, KK must be a simplex by the following lemma due to Rogers and Shephard.

Lemma 4 from [11]. Let KK be a convex body in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. If the intersections K∩(K+x)K\cap(K+x) are homothetic for all x∈K−Kx\in K-K, then KK is a simplex.

Finally, in order to show that 00 is a vertex of KK, note that equality holds also in (16)(\ref{eq:C-versus-(K-L)}), for the bodies (1−λ)​K,λ​K(1-\lambda)K,\lambda K. Hence, among all sections of C⁡((1−λ)​K,λ​K)C((1-\lambda)K,\lambda K) parallel to H=E∩C⁡((1−λ)​K,λ​K)H=E\cap C((1-\lambda)K,\lambda K), HH is the only one with unit length. Since we assumed that KK contains the origin, one has (1−λ)​K∩−λ​K={0}(1-\lambda)K\cap-\lambda K=\{0\}. This, together with the fact that KK is a simplex, means that 00 must be one of the vertices of KK.

We turn now to show that equality in Theorem 1.6 holds if and only if KK and LL are simplices with a common vertex at the origin, and such that (1−θ)​L=θ​K(1-\theta)L=\theta K. To this end, we shall make use of Theorem 1.9. Assume that for some given θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1),

Vol⁡(L∨−K)​Vol​(θ​K∩(1−θ)​L)=Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L).{\rm Vol}(L\vee-K)\,{\rm Vol}(\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L)={\rm Vol}(K){\rm Vol}(L). (18)

Since the inclusion θ​K∩(1−θ)​L⊆(K∘+L∘)∘\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L\subseteq\left(K^{\circ}+L^{\circ}\right)^{\circ} always holds, by Theorem 1.9 we then must have

θ​K∩(1−θ)​L=(K∘+L∘)∘\theta K\cap(1-\theta)L=\left(K^{\circ}+L^{\circ}\right)^{\circ}

(as both are compact convex sets, inclusion together with equality of volumes implies equality of sets). We claim that this equality implies that KK and LL are homothetic. Indeed, we may rewrite the above equality as

θ−1​K∘∨(1−θ)−1​L∘=K∘+L∘,\theta^{-1}K^{\circ}\vee(1-\theta)^{-1}L^{\circ}=K^{\circ}+L^{\circ},

so that in particular

θ−1​K∘⊂K∘+L∘,(1−θ)−1​L∘⊂K∘+L∘.\theta^{-1}K^{\circ}\subset K^{\circ}+L^{\circ},\qquad(1-\theta)^{-1}L^{\circ}\subset K^{\circ}+L^{\circ}.

Thus, θ−1​hK∘≤hK∘+hL∘\theta^{-1}h_{K^{\circ}}\leq h_{K^{\circ}}+h_{L^{\circ}}, and (1−θ)−1​hL∘≤hK∘+hL∘(1-\theta)^{-1}h_{L^{\circ}}\leq h_{K^{\circ}}+h_{L^{\circ}}. Putting the two together one has

hL∘=1−θθ​hK∘,h_{L^{\circ}}=\frac{1-\theta}{\theta}h_{K^{\circ}},

or equivalently, (1−θ)​L=θ​K(1-\theta)L=\theta K. This, together with (18)(\ref{eq-in-1.6}) implies that equality in (7)(\ref{ineq-needed-for-God}) holds for KK. Thus, from the characterization of the equality case in Theorem 1.5, the body KK must be a simplex with a vertex at the origin. This completes the proof for the equality case in Theorem 1.6.

Remark 5.3.

It is worthwhile to notice that in Theorem 1.9 there are more equality cases than in Theorem 1.5. Indeed, one may readily check that for positive λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n}, and the bodies K=conv⁡{0,e1,…,en}K={\rm conv}\{0,e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\}, L=conv⁡{0,λ1​e1,…,λn}L={\rm conv}\{0,\lambda_{1}e_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}\} we have that Vol⁡(K)​Vol​(L)=1n!2​∏i=1nλi{\rm Vol}(K){\rm Vol}(L)=\frac{1}{n!^{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}, that

Vol⁡((K∘+L∘)∘)=1n!​∏i=1nλi1+λi{\rm Vol}(\left(K^{\circ}+L^{\circ}\right)^{\circ})=\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{1+\lambda_{i}}

and that

Vol⁡(K∨−L)=1n!​∑A⊂{1,…​n}∏i∈Aλi=1n!​∏i=1n(1+λi).{\rm Vol}(K\vee-L)=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{A\subset\{1,\ldots n\}}\prod_{i\in A}\lambda_{i}=\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+\lambda_{i}).

The characterization of the equality case in Theorem 1.9 is thus left open.
